title: Natural English
topic: Storytelling: Connectors & Expressions for Natural Speech

sections.title: 1. Why This Class Exists
sections.content:
The **Natural English** Friday class focuses on the small details that make spoken English sound fluent and authentic — not academic or forced.

> Traditional classes teach grammar and vocabulary for writing. This class trains the *connectors and expressions* that native speakers use automatically in conversation.

**The shadowing technique:** Imitate what you hear as closely as possible — repeat words out loud, mimic rhythm and intonation. The goal is to make new expressions feel comfortable *before* you need them in a real conversation, so they sound organic, not rehearsed.

Today's focus: **storytelling** — expressions that make an anecdote flow naturally, organised into four categories.

sections.title: 2. Introducing Unexpected Events
sections.content:
Use these when something surprising happens in your story:

| Expression | Example |
|---|---|
| **All of a sudden** | *I was giving a class and **all of a sudden** the ceiling broke in half.* |
| **Out of nowhere** | *I was walking down the street and **out of nowhere** this man came up to me.* |

> **Out of the blue** (mentioned by a student) is also correct but less common as a story connector.

Both expressions go at the beginning of the clause that introduces the surprise.

sections.title: 3. Introducing Surprising or Contrasting Information
sections.content:
Use these when you reveal something unexpected relative to what you just said — the English equivalent of *resulta que...* or *¿lo que son las cosas?*

| Expression | Notes |
|---|---|
| **Believe it or not** | Placed at the start: *Believe it or not, he was from Kathmandu.* |
| **Turns out** | Always in present form, even for past events. Placed at the start: *I thought he was from China, but turns out he was from Kathmandu.* |

**Key rule for *turns out*:** Do not conjugate it. It is a fixed expression — never *turned out that*, always just **turns out** followed by the clause.

> *Turns out* = Spanish *resulta que* — very natural and very common in spoken English.

sections.title: 4. Moving the Story Forward
sections.content:
Use these to transition between parts of a story — the spoken equivalent of academic connectors like *furthermore* or *subsequently*, but natural and colloquial.

| Expression | Notes |
|---|---|
| **Then** | The classic, always correct. |
| **So** | Very natural; also signals a slight change of direction. |
| **Anyway** | Closes one part of the story and opens the next — equivalent of Spanish *en fin* or *bueno*. |
| **Next thing I knew** | Jumps to the following action: *I was walking down the street and next thing I knew I was at the beach.* |

**Anyway vs Anyways:**
- Use **anyway** as a story connector (*Anyway, I went to the beach with my friends*).
- *Anyways* is very colloquial and mainly used at the end of a sentence meaning *de todas formas* (*you are busy anyways*). Best to stick with *anyway* for everything — it works in both positions.

sections.title: 5. Showing Your Feelings
sections.content:
Use these to express your emotions or evaluation while telling the story — making it subjective and engaging.

**Expressing honesty / sincerity:**

| Expression | Notes |
|---|---|
| **To be honest** | Very common: *To be honest, that affected me a lot.* |
| **Honestly** | Interchangeable: *Honestly, that affected me a lot.* |
| **To tell the truth** | Slightly more formal but also natural. |

**Expressing good or bad outcomes:**

| Expression | Notes |
|---|---|
| **Luckily** / **Fortunately** | *Luckily, everything was okay.* |
| **Unfortunately** | *Unfortunately, he was missing a leg.* |

**Pronunciation of *unfortunately*:** Many syllables — stress the second syllable.

> un · **for** · tu · nate · ly → *un-FOR-chu-nit-lee*

Practise in slow motion: **un — for — tu — nate — ly**, then speed up.

**Luck vs lack (pronunciation note):**
- **luck** (good fortune): brighter, more open vowel
- **lack** (absence of something): slightly more closed
- In British English the difference is subtle; in American English it is more distinct (*lack* sounds like *lak*).
- Context always makes the meaning clear — don't overthink it.

qs.q: You are telling a story. A man suddenly appeared from nowhere and spoke to you. Which expression best introduces this?
opts: Believe it or not, a man appeared.
All of a sudden, a man appeared.
To be honest, a man appeared.
qs.ans: All of a sudden, a man appeared.

qs.q: You thought he was from China, but he was actually from Kathmandu. Which expression best introduces this contrast?
opts: Next thing I knew, he was from Kathmandu.
Turns out he was from Kathmandu.
qs.ans: Turns out he was from Kathmandu.

qs.q: How should you use 'turns out' when talking about a past event?
opts: Turned out that he was late.
It turned out he was late.
Turns out that it was late.

sections.title: 1. Warm-Up Translations
sections.content:
| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Nos lo hemos pasado muy bien. | We've had a great time. |
| Gracias por todo lo que has hecho. | Thank you for everything you've done. |
| ¿Qué haría yo sin tu ayuda? | What would I do without your help? |
| Lo hice yo mismo. | I did it myself. |
| No lo puedo levantar. | I can't lift it. |
| Tendrás que hablar más alto. | You'll have to speak louder. |
| Démosle otra oportunidad. | Let's give him another chance. |
| Nos quedan tres horas. | We have three hours left. |
| ¿Ha habido unos cambios recientemente? | There have been some changes lately. |
| Le gusta su trabajo. | He likes his job. |

**Notes from class:**

- **Lo hice yo mismo** → *I did it **myself*** (emphasis: *you* were the one who did it) vs. *I did it **by myself*** (emphasis: you were *alone*). \nExample: *I did all the driving myself* = I was the driver · *I drove there by myself* = I was alone in the car.
- **Nos quedan tres horas** → *We have three hours **left*** — "quedar" often translates to "have ... left".
- **Lately / recientemente** → these time expressions almost always trigger the **Present Perfect**: *there **have been** some changes lately* ✓ · ~~there were~~ ✗
- **Overuse of "to stay"**: Don't say *"I am staying at home"* for *estoy en mi casa*. Just say *"I'm at home"* / *"I'm at school"* / *"I'm at the office"* — no "staying" needed.

sections.title: 2. Work vs. Job
sections.content:
Both translate to *trabajo* in Spanish, but they follow a **countable / uncountable** rule.

**As a verb — always *work*:**

| Spanish | ✓ English |
|---|---|
| Trabaja en una fábrica. | He **works** in a factory. |
| Está trabajando. | He's **working**. |
| Empieza a trabajar temprano. | He starts **work** early. |

**As a noun:**

| Situation | Use | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **Uncountable** (quality / effort / concept) | *work* | She does very good **work**. |
| **Countable** (specific positions) | *job* | He has two **jobs**. |

- *I like my **job**.* → Countable — a specific position.
- *My brother has a good **job**.* → Countable.
- *He does very good **work**.* → Uncountable — referring to quality.

**Exception — "the works of Shakespeare":** In the sense of *obras de arte*, "work" is countable: *the **works** of Shakespeare*, *beautiful **works** of art*.

**Quick rule:** If you can count it with a number → *job(s)*. If it refers to effort or the concept → *work*.

sections.title: 3. Present Perfect Simple vs. Continuous
sections.content:
Both use *have/has*, but the continuous adds *been + -ing*. The key difference: **action verbs** + whether the action **continues into the future**.

### When to use Present Perfect Continuous

You need **two things**:
1. An **action verb** (not a stative verb)
2. The idea that the action **is ongoing / will continue**

| ✓ Correct | ✗ Wrong |
|---|---|
| I've been **sitting** here for 10 minutes. | ~~I've been knowing~~ her for years. |
| I've been **living** in Spain for 23 years. | ~~I've been having~~ this car since 2010. |
| They've been **playing** together since 1963. | ~~I've been understanding~~ English. |

### Stative verbs — always use Simple

Stative verbs describe a **state**, not an action. They cannot take *-ing* here:

- **know** → I've **known** her for five years. *(not "been knowing")*
- **have** (possession) → He's **had** this car for ten years.
- **like, love, want, understand** → same rule.

### Transition moments (the airplane example)

Kyle's example: imagine you're moving back to Canada, on a plane leaving Spain.

> **Before take-off** (still in Spain → Present Perfect):
> *"I've **lived** here for 23 years and it's been wonderful."*

> **After take-off** (Spain is in the past → Simple Past):
> *"I **lived** in Spain for 23 years. It **was** good. I **had** a great time. I **met** a lot of people."*

The key skill: **recognise those moments of tense transition** (*reconocer esos momentos de cambio en tiempo verbal*).

### Lately / recently → always Present Perfect

- *There **have been** some changes lately.* ✓
- ~~There were some changes lately.~~ ✗

### How long ...? — Practice examples

| Question / Statement | Tense | Why |
|---|---|---|
| I've **known** Jose Luis for four years. | PPS | "know" = stative |
| I've been **sitting** in this chair for 40 minutes. | PPCO | action verb, ongoing |
| The Rolling Stones **have been** together since 1963. | PPCO | ongoing state |
| James Dean **was** alive from 1932 to 1956. | Simple Past | finished period |
| Spain **has had** a constitution since 1978. | PPS | "have" = stative |
| I **met** you two years ago. | Simple Past | single past event |
| I've **known** you for two years. | PPS | ongoing state from that point |

*PPS = Present Perfect Simple · PPCO = Present Perfect Continuous*

sections.title: 4. Phrasal Verbs with 'pick'
sections.content:
### pick up

Two main meanings:

**1. To retrieve** something from the floor / ground
- *I dropped my pen and **picked it up**.*
- **floor** (inside) vs. **ground** (outside): *the pen fell on the **floor*** · *I dropped my keys on the **ground** outside.*

**2. To collect** someone from a location
- *Can you **pick me up** at the airport?*
- *I'll **pick** you **up** at nine.*

---

### pick out

To **choose / select** from options (= *escoger*)
- *It took me a long time to **pick out** a shirt.*
- *I need to **pick out** a new song for the podcast.*

---

### pick on

To **tease, harass, or bully** someone (= *meterse con*, *molestar*)
- *They're always **picking on** him at school.*
- *Don't **pick on** your little brother.*

---

### Bonus — pickpocket (noun)

**pickpocket** = *carterista* — a thief who steals from pockets on the metro, etc.
- *Be careful of **pickpockets** on the subway.*

---

**Quick summary:**

| Phrasal verb | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| pick up | retrieve from floor; collect someone | *Pick it up · Pick me up at 8* |
| pick out | choose / select | *Pick out a shirt* |
| pick on | tease / harass / bully | *Stop picking on him* |

sections.title: 1. Warm-Up Translations (Business English)
sections.content:
Business-themed translation exercise.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Comprendo perfectamente tu/su política | I perfectly understand your policy |
| Quisiera que me mandara una copia | I would like you to send me a copy |
| El acuerdo está claro en este punto | The agreement is clear on this point |
| Lleva dos meses en vigor | It has been in force for two months |
| Lo siento pero no podemos hacer nada | I'm sorry but we can't do anything |
| Tengo que devolverte la factura | I have to return the invoice to you |
| Emite/Expide una nueva sin la mano de obra | Issue a new one without labor |
| La pagaremos cuando la recibamos | We'll pay you when we receive it |
| Cursaremos la factura sin demora | We will process the invoice without delay |
| Es un placer hacer negocios con usted | It's a pleasure doing business with you |

### Key vocabulary

**Política** has two meanings:
- *policy*: política de privacidad = privacy policy
- *politics*: No soy política porque no me gusta la política = I'm not a politician because I don't like politics

**On this point** — not *in* this point. The agreement is clear **on** this point.

**In force** (two words) vs **to enforce** (one word):
- A law that is active = *the law is in force*
- To make people obey it = *the police enforce the law*

**Double negative** — avoid it in English:
- ✗ *We can't do nothing.*    ✓ *We can't do anything.*

**To issue** (expedir, emitir) — also used as a noun: *an issue of a magazine*

**Labor / Labour** — American English drops the U (*labor*); British English keeps it (*labour*). Same pattern: *favor/favour*, *color/colour*.

**To process the invoice** — more common than *to expedite the invoice*.

**It's a pleasure doing business with you** — use the gerund (*doing*), not the infinitive (*to do*).

sections.title: 2. Prepositions of Place
sections.content:
Describing where objects are in a room.

### Key prepositions

| Preposition | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| on | encima de (en contacto) | The dog is **on** the armchair |
| under | debajo de | The small dog is **under** the table |
| next to | al lado de | There is a pencil **next to** the small dog |
| between | entre (dos cosas) | The small pencil is **between** the book and the glass |
| on top of | encima de (sobre) | The phone is **on top of** the magazine |
| in the back of | en la parte de atrás de | The small table is **in the back of** the room |
| in the front of | en la parte delantera de | — |

### Vocabulary: furniture & objects

- **Armchair** — a single chair with arms; also called a *lazy boy* (the reclining kind)
- **Couch / Sofa** — seats multiple people; *armchair* is for one person
- **Newspaper** — not to be confused with *magazine* (revista)
- **Radio cassette player** — reproductor de radio y casete

### Using articles correctly

When describing a specific item already established in context, use **the**:
- *The big dog is on the armchair. The small dog is under the table.*
- Introduce a new item with **a/an**, then refer back with **the**.

sections.title: 3. Possessive Pronouns
sections.content:
Spanish uses *el mío / el tuyo / el de Pepe* — English uses independent possessive pronouns (no article needed).

| Spanish | English | Example |
|---|---|---|
| el mío / la mía | mine | *Where's mine?* (never *where's the mine*) |
| el tuyo / la tuya | yours | *Why are yours bigger than mine?* |
| el suyo / la suya (él) | his | *Mine and his are very similar.* |
| el suyo / la suya (ella) | hers | *Theirs is the same colour as hers.* |
| el nuestro / la nuestra | ours | *Ours weren't chosen.* (not *our ones*) |
| el suyo / la suya (ellos) | theirs | *Theirs is the blue one.* |
| el de Pepe | Pepe's | *Pepe's won't arrive until the end of the month.* |

### Common mistakes
- ✗ *Where's the mine?*    ✓ *Where's mine?*
- ✗ *It's from Pepe / It's of Pepe*    ✓ *It's Pepe's.*
- ✗ *Our ones weren't chosen.*    ✓ *Ours weren't chosen.*

### Whose

*¿De quién?* = **Whose** — the noun goes immediately after:

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| ¿De quién es este libro? | Whose book is this? |
| ¿De quién es este vaso? | Whose glass is this? |
| ¿De quiénes eran los que vi ayer? | Whose were the ones I saw yesterday? |

### Used to + possessives

*Antes era mío, pero ahora es de Pepe.* → **It used to be mine, but now it's Pepe's.**

*Antes* signals habitual/repeated past → use **used to**:
- *It used to be mine, but now it's his.*
- *I used to eat more fish.*

sections.title: 4. Word Order: The Next · The Last · The First + Number
sections.content:
In Spanish the number can come before or after *próximo/último*. In English the order is always fixed.

### Rule

> **the** + **next / last / first** + **number / few** + **noun**

| Spanish | ✗ Wrong | ✓ Correct |
|---|---|---|
| las tres próximas semanas | the three next weeks | **the next three weeks** |
| los últimos cinco minutos | the five last minutes | **the last five minutes** |
| los próximos días | the few next days | **the next few days** |
| los últimos días | the few last days | **the last few days** |

### Examples
- *I'll be away for the **next three weeks**.*
- *We talked about grammar for the **last five minutes** of class.*
- *She's been sick for the **last few days**.*
- *There will be lots of classes over the **next few weeks**.*
- *My camera broke and I couldn't take any photos on the **last two days** of my holiday.*

### Memory tip

Think: *which ones?* (next / last / first) → *how many?* (three / few) → *what?* (weeks / days).

sections.title: 5. Linking & Natural Speech
sections.content:
Natural spoken English links words together, especially when a word ends in a consonant and the next starts with a vowel.

### Are you → 'are ya'

In everyday speech, *are you* blends into a single sound:

| Written | Natural spoken |
|---|---|
| Are you going to call him? | *Are ya gonna call him?* |
| Are you thinking about work? | *Are ya thinking about work?* |
| Are you going to the party? | *Are ya going to the party?* |
| Are you going on holiday this summer? | *Are ya going on holiday this summer?* |
| Are you learning? Are you practising? | *Are ya learning? Are ya practising?* |

### Common reductions

| Full form | Reduced | Spanish equivalent |
|---|---|---|
| going to | **gonna** | ir a |
| want to | **wanna** | querer |

### How to train it

It's not just *learning* — it's **training**. Through repetition, the right structures and pronunciation become automatic (*sin pensarlo*):
- Hear it → repeat it → internalize it
- *Are ya gonna call him?* — say it until it flows naturally.

topic: Behind the World Cup

sections.title: 1. Discussion: Impossible Choices
sections.content:
Two discussion questions to kick off the class.

**Choice 1:** You can only save one — which survives?
- 🇧🇷 Brazil's **five** World Cup titles
- 🇪🇸 Spain's **2010** World Cup

The other one disappears from history forever!

---

**Choice 2:** Your country reaches the World Cup final. Would you rather…
- 🏟️ Watch the match **live at the stadium** (all expenses paid)
- 💶 Receive **€10,000**

Which would you choose and why?

sections.title: 2. What Is the World Cup Really About?
sections.content:
The World Cup is not just about football. Which of these six things do you think matters most?

| | Purpose | What it means |
|---|---|---|
| 🎭 | **Entertainment** | People love the drama and excitement |
| 💰 | **Money** | Billions spent and earned — by countries, brands and players |
| 🏳️ | **National identity** | A chance to feel proud of where you come from |

sections.title: 1. Warm-Up Translations (Marketing)
sections.content:
A marketing-themed translation exercise.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Me falta la información apropiada | I lack the right information |
| Documenta todo lo que hagas | Document / Keep track of / Keep record of everything you do |
| Una buena información es una potente herramienta de marketing | Good information is a powerful marketing tool |
| Analizamos los resultados diarios de las ventas | We analyze the daily sales results / sales performance |
| Es un placer hacer negocios con usted | It's a pleasure doing business with you |
| Puedes comprar información de proveedores externos | You can buy / purchase information from external suppliers |
| No suelen ofrecer facilidades de pago | They don't usually offer credit terms / payment terms |
| Necesito la información apropiada en el momento propicio | I need the right information at the right time |
| Hemos realizado una encuesta entre secretarias | We've conducted a survey among secretaries |

### Key vocabulary

**To lack** (faltar) — used for abstract deficiencies:
- *This food lacks salt.* · *I lack the right information.*

**Information** — uncountable in English. Never say *a good information*. Say *good information*.

**Performance** — can translate *resultados* when referring to output: *daily sales performance*.

**Purchase** — more formal synonym for *buy*.

**Supplier vs Provider:**
- A **supplier** supplies a physical product → to **customers**
- A **provider** provides a service → to **clients**

**Credit terms / Payment terms** = facilidades de pago

**To conduct a survey** = realizar una encuesta

**Pronunciation note:** *apropiada* → English *appropriate* — single R, different stress.

sections.title: 2. Passive Voice
sections.content:
The passive voice is **not a change in tense** — it's a change in **voice**. It presents the same information from a different angle.

### When to use it
- To **emphasise a subject** that would otherwise be the object: *Rafa Nadal is being beaten by an amateur.*
- To **de-emphasise the agent**: *You're fired.* (not "I am firing you")

### Structure
> **to be** (in the correct tense) + **past participle**

The verb *to be* carries the tense; the main verb stays in the past participle (3rd form).

| Tense | Active | Passive |
|---|---|---|
| Present continuous | The amateur is beating Rafa | Rafa **is being beaten** by the amateur |
| Simple past | An amateur beat Rafa | Rafa **was beaten** by an amateur |
| Future | Someone will beat Rafa | Rafa **will be beaten** |
| Present perfect | Someone has proposed improvements | Improvements **have been proposed** |
| Past perfect | Someone had mentioned the password | The password **had been mentioned** |

### Practice sentences
1. Someone handed me a note → **I was handed a note** / *A note was handed to me.*
2. Someone offered her a secondhand bicycle → **She was offered a secondhand bicycle.**
3. Someone has proposed improvements to the developers → **Improvements have been proposed to the developers.**
4. Someone suggested some interesting changes to me → **Some interesting changes were suggested to me.**
5. Someone awarded him a prize → **He was awarded a prize.**
6. Someone will announce the president's arrival to the waiting journalists → **The president's arrival will be announced to the waiting journalists.**
7. Someone had mentioned the password to the thieves → **The password had been mentioned to the thieves.**
8. Someone has lent me some skis → **I have been lent some skis.**
9. Someone is sending me a lot of spam emails → **A lot of spam emails are being sent to me.**
10. Someone is going to explain the changes to the students → **The changes are going to be explained to the students.**

sections.title: 3. Present Perfect vs Simple Past (Reading Analysis)
sections.content:
Read this paragraph and notice how tenses alternate — each choice follows a logical rule:

> *I've been here for **one month**. I haven't done much to my apartment **yet**, but I've met the neighbors. I invited them round for coffee **yesterday**. They're really nice. I also joined a gym **on my first day** here and I've been almost every day **since then**. Last night I went out for a meal with some girls from my exercise class and it was great fun. I've **just** ordered some new furniture and I bought some paint for the living room **two weeks ago**, but I haven't had time to start painting **yet**.*

### Why each tense is used

| Sentence | Tense | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| I've been here **for a month** | Present perfect | *for* + period of time — ongoing situation |
| I **haven't** done much **yet** | Present perfect | *yet* in negatives/questions |
| I've met the neighbors | Present perfect | action within the ongoing period, no specific moment given |
| I invited them round **yesterday** | Simple past | specific isolated moment in the past |
| I joined a gym **on my first day** | Simple past | pinpointed past moment |
| I've been almost every day **since then** | Present perfect | *since then* — from a past point up to now |
| I've **just** ordered furniture | Present perfect | *just* = acabar de |
| I bought paint **two weeks ago** | Simple past | *ago* = specific past point |
| I **haven't** had time **yet** | Present perfect | *yet* in negative |

### British vs American English
- **Invite round** (British) = **invite over** (American): *I invited them round for coffee.*
- **Great fun** — typical British expression: *It was great fun.*

sections.title: 4. Phrasal Verbs: Look Down On / Look Up To
sections.content:
Two contrasting phrasal verbs about respect and admiration.

### To look down on someone
**= to despise / to disrespect / to think less of someone**

- *She always feels that people are looking down on her.*
- *It's important not to look down on anyone.*
- Note: preposition is **on**, not *to*

### To look up to someone
**= to admire / to respect someone as a role model**

- *I look up to my parents.*
- *I look up to hard-working people.*
- *Who do you look up to?*
- Note: preposition is **to**, not *on*

> These are not true opposites: *look down on* = active disrespect; *look up to* = admiration of a specific person.

### Soap box
A **soap box** is the figurative platform from which someone broadcasts a message to many people. From the old English park tradition where people literally stood on wooden crates (*cajas de jabón*) to give speeches.

- *Celebrities have a soap box they can stand on — with that comes a responsibility.*

| This monastery was built **in the 12th century**. | **When** was this monastery built? |

### Notes
- Passive sentences keep the question word; the auxiliary stays passive: *When **was** this monastery built?*
- Keep the preposition at the end: *When will she be operated **on**?* · *What can you trust him **for**?*

sections.title: 1. While & Whilst
sections.content:
Two words that both mean *mientras* — identical in meaning, different in register.

| Word | Register | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **while** | Standard / neutral | The everyday word |
| **whilst** | Formal / elevated | Very British — same meaning, different ending |

Just swapping *while* for *whilst* automatically elevates your speech without any complex structure.

### Don't confuse with…

| Word | Meaning | Use |
|---|---|---|
| **whereas** | *Mientras que* (contrast) | Expresses opposition between two facts: *I'm blonde whereas he's dark-haired* |
| **meanwhile** | *Mientras tanto* | Standalone expression — beginning/end of a sentence, not a connector |
| **in the meantime** | *Mientras tanto* | Same as *meanwhile* — standalone expression |

> **Key rule:** *while* / *whilst* connect two simultaneous actions. *Meanwhile* / *in the meantime* stand alone. *Whereas* expresses contrast.

### Structure

- while/whilst + subject + verb: *Can we discuss it **whilst** we drive to Madrid?*
- while/whilst + -ing (same subject): *I did my homework **while** listening to music.*

### Practice sentences
- Did you fall asleep while reading the novel? → Yes, I **fell** asleep while reading the novel.
- Can we discuss it whilst driving to Madrid? → Yes, we can discuss it whilst driving to Madrid.
- What did you say to her whilst you were cooking? → I said something to her whilst I was cooking.
- Would you like something to drink while you're waiting? → Yes, I would like something to drink while I'm waiting.
- Did the phone ring while we were having dinner? → Yes, the phone **rang** while we were having dinner.
- Did you do your homework while listening to music? → Yes, I did my homework while listening to music.
- Did your son get scared whilst he rode the pony? → Yes, my son **got scared** whilst he rode the pony.
- Did you read the book whilst laying on the sofa? → Yes, I **read** /rɛd/ the book whilst laying on the sofa.

### Irregular verb reminders
- **fall** → past: **fell** *(not 'felt' — that's the past of 'feel')*
- **ring** → past: **rang**
- **read** → past: **read** *(same spelling, pronounced /rɛd/ — like 'rojo')*

sections.title: 2. Silent T Pronunciation
sections.content:
In English, some words contain a **T that is completely silent** — ignore it as if it weren't there.

This is especially common in verbs. Accidentally pronouncing the T is a very typical mistake.

### Silent T verbs

| Verb | Pronunciation | Spanish | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| **glisten** | /ˈɡlɪsən/ | resplandecer, brillar con destellos | More specific than *shine* (= brillar general) |
| **soften** | /ˈsɒfən/ | suavizarse, ablandarse | From adj. *soft* — ⚠ *soft* /sɒft/ HAS a T; *soften* does NOT |
| **whistle** | /ˈwɪsəl/ | silbar | |
| **fasten** | /ˈfɑːsən/ | abrochar, sujetar | *Fasten your seatbelt* = abrochar el cinturón |
| **rustle** | /ˈrʌsəl/ | crujir, susurrar | The sound leaves make in the wind |

### Important distinction: soft vs soften
- **soft** *(adjective)* → /sɒft/ — **pronounce the T**
- **soften** *(verb)* → /ˈsɒfən/ — **silent T**

### Pronunciation of *jewellery*
Trick: think of the Spanish word *chulería* — say it with an English accent and drop the Spanish flavour → **jewellery** /ˈdʒuːəlri/

### Practice questions
- Is your new jewellery glistening?
- Has your dad softened since he's been retired?
- Do you know how to whistle?
- Do you always fasten your seatbelt when you travel by car?
- Can you hear the leaves rustling in the forest?

sections.title: 4. Pronunciation: -ed Endings on Adjectives
sections.content:
When adjectives are formed with **-ed**, the ending does NOT always add a new syllable.

| Word | Pronunciation | Rule |
|---|---|---|
| **striped** | /straɪpt/ | -ed → **t** (after voiceless consonant *p*) |
| **checked** | /tʃekt/ | -ed → **t** (after voiceless consonant *k*) |
| **patterned** | /ˈpætərnd/ | -ed → **d** (after voiced consonant *n*) |

**Floral:** /ˈflɔːrəl/ — the 'o' is a close, rounded sound. Avoid the open 'a': ~~flAral~~ ✗ → **floral** ✓

> Rule of thumb for -ed endings: after voiceless consonants (p, k, s, ch…) → **/t/**; after voiced sounds → **/d/**; after *t* or *d* → **/ɪd/** (adds a syllable, e.g. *wanted*, *needed*).

sections.title: 5. Irregular Plural: Scarf → Scarves
sections.content:
Nouns ending in **-f** or **-fe** usually form the plural by changing to **-ves**:

| Singular | Plural |
|---|---|
| scarf | **scarves** |
| half | **halves** |
| leaf | **leaves** |
| life | **lives** |
| knife | **knives** |
| wife | **wives** |

> Remove the *f* and add **ves** — not just *s*.

sections.title: 6. Question Formation: Ask me if / Ask me whether
sections.content:
**"Ask me if"** and **"ask me whether"** are interchangeable — both introduce an indirect question. The answer is a direct question in normal question word order.

| Instruction | Direct question |
|---|---|
| Ask me if I own a leather jacket | **Do you own** a leather jacket? |
| Ask me when I last wore denim jeans | **When did you last wear** denim jeans? |
| Ask me whether I prefer cotton or polyester | **Do you prefer** cotton or polyester? |
| Ask me if I would wear a silk shirt to work | **Would you wear** a silk shirt to work? |
| Ask me which material I wear most often | **Which material do you wear** most often? |
| Ask me if I have anything made of corduroy | **Do you have** anything made of corduroy? |
| Ask me whether linen is practical in winter | **Is linen** practical in winter? |
| Ask me what I usually wear at home | **What do you usually wear** at home? |
| Ask me if expensive clothes are always better | **Are expensive clothes** always better? |

> *If* and *whether* are both correct in these instructions — don't be confused when you see both used interchangeably.

sections.content:
| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| ¿Qué te pasa ahora? | What's the **matter** with you now? |
| Voy a retorcerte el cuello | I'm going to **wring** your neck |
| Me estás haciendo la vida imposible | You're making my life **miserable** |
| Parece que me estás castigando | It seems like you're **punishing** me |
| Creí que se cortó la línea | I thought we **got cut off** |
| Tenemos que recortar gastos | We have to **cut back on** expenses |
| ¿Qué conclusión sacaste de esto? | What conclusion did you **draw** from this? |
| Tenemos que recurrir a financiación externa | We had to **resort to** outside financing |
| ¿Cómo puedes soportar esa clase de arte? | How can you **stand** that kind of art? |
| Si sigues intentando a la larga tendrás éxito | If you keep trying, you'll **eventually** succeed |
| Como se fueron hace una hora, no creo que puedas alcanzarles | Since they left an hour ago, I **don't think** you can **catch up with** them |

---

### Key notes

**To wring** — spelled W-R-I-N-G (not *ring*). To twist and squeeze something.
- *to wring out* a cloth = escurrir un trapo
- *to wring someone's neck* = retorcerle el cuello a alguien (dramatic expression)

**"I don't think" + affirmative** is preferred over **"I think" + negative**:
- ~~I think you won't be able to catch up with them.~~ ✗
- **I don't think you'll be able to catch up with them.** ✓

**Catch up with / Catch up on:**
- *catch up **with** someone* = alcanzar a alguien (physically)
- *catch up **on** something* = ponerse al día en algo
> *I need to catch up on my reading. I need to catch up with him.*

sections.title: 2. Vocabulary: Draw — Multiple Meanings
sections.content:
The word **draw** has many different uses in English:

| Use | Spanish | Example |
|---|---|---|
| to draw (a picture) | dibujar | *She's drawing a portrait.* |
| a draw (result) | un empate | *The match ended in a draw.* |
| to draw (attention) | atraer | *The noise drew everyone's attention.* |
| to draw (water from a well) | sacar | *They drew water from the well.* |
| to draw a conclusion | sacar una conclusión | *What conclusion do you draw from this?* |
| to withdraw / draw out (money) | sacar dinero del banco | *I need to withdraw some cash. / Draw out some money.* |
| a drawback | un inconveniente / punto negativo | *The main drawback is the cost.* |

> **Win, Lose or Draw** — a classic game show where *draw* plays on both meanings: to sketch AND to tie.

sections.title: 3. Stand vs. Put up with / Resort to / Reach out to
sections.content:
### Stand vs. Put up with

Both mean *soportar / aguantar*, but there is a subtle difference:

| Expression | Best used for | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **can't stand** | Things, sensations, tastes, types of people | *I can't stand the taste of pineapple.* / *I can't stand noisy neighbours.* |
| **can't put up with** | Behaviour, ongoing situations | *I can't put up with that behaviour.* / *I'll have to put up with it.* |

> Both overlap in many cases. The fine point: you *can't stand* a thing; you *have to put up with* an action or ongoing situation.

---

### Resort to

**To resort to** = recurrir a (usually to something undesirable or last-resort)

> *We had to resort to outside financing.*

---

### Reach out to

**To reach out to** someone = intentar establecer contacto con alguien

> *Reach out to me if you need any help.*

Don't confuse with *catch up with* (alcanzar físicamente) or *reach* (llegar).

sections.title: 4. Grammar: Uses of ONE (el/la que, los/las que)
sections.content:
**ONE** / **ONES** replace a noun already mentioned to avoid repetition — equivalent to Spanish *el/la que* and *los/las que*.

### Examples

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| El que está en la mesa es de ellos | **The one** on the table is theirs |
| El tuyo es el que rechazamos | Yours is **the one** we rejected |
| Este y aquel son de ella | **This one** and **that one** are hers |
| ¿Cuál te gusta más? | Which **one** do you like best? |
| Prefiero el que me enseñaste ayer | I prefer **the one** you showed me yesterday |
| ¿Cuál quieres? ¿El de la mesa o el de la silla? | Which one do you want? **The one** on the table or **the one** on the chair? |
| Los míos son los verdes | Mine are **the green ones** |

---

### Possessive pronouns — never use "the" before them

| Spanish | Wrong ✗ | Correct ✓ |
|---|---|---|
| El mío | ~~The mine~~ | **Mine** |
| Los míos son los verdes | ~~The mines are the green ones~~ | **Mine are the green ones** |
| La de ellos sigue perdida | — | **Theirs** is still lost |

> *Mine, yours, his, hers, ours, theirs* — these stand alone. No article, no change for singular/plural.

---

### These / Those — "ones" optional

*Estos y aquellos son míos* → **These and those are mine** (or: *these ones and those ones* — both correct, but the shorter form is more natural).

sections.title: 5. Supposed to — Three Uses  ★ Main topic
sections.content:
**Supposed to** has three main uses in English:

---

### 1. Obligation / Expected behaviour

Equivalent to *se supone que* (deber, tener que).

- *You're supposed to wear a tie at work.*
- *What time are we supposed to be there?*
- *Am I supposed to bring anything to eat?*
- *Are you supposed to wear a seat belt?*

---

### 2. Past unfulfilled expectation

Used with **was / were supposed to** — something that was expected but may not have happened.

- *Was I supposed to call you after class?*
- *She was supposed to be here at 9.*
- *Was I supposed to be in the meeting?*

---

### 3. Reputation / "People say that..."

Equivalent to *se dice que / dicen que / se supone que es...* — based on what others say or general expectation.

- *He's supposed to be great at telling jokes.* (= dicen que es buenísimo contando chistes)
- *Isn't this supposed to be a safe city?*
- *Isn't this movie supposed to be scary?*
- *Spain is supposed to be one of the best teams.*
- *These classes are supposed to be good for your English.*

sections.title: 6. Trip vs. Travel vs. Journey
sections.content:
These three words all relate to *viaje* in Spanish, but they are not interchangeable:

| Word | Part of speech | Spanish | Use |
|---|---|---|---|
| **trip** | noun | viaje (ida y vuelta) | A specific journey, usually with a return; the whole experience |
| **travel** | verb / gerund | viajar | The general action of going from place to place |
| **journey** | noun | trayecto / viaje (aventurero) | The act of traveling itself — often implies length, difficulty, or adventure |

---

### Examples

- *Have a nice **trip**!* — greeting before someone leaves
- *I took a **trip** to Calpe in April.* — specific round trip
- *I love **traveling**.* — the general activity
- *We've **traveled** a great distance.* — the verb in action
- ***The journey** was tiring, but it was a great **trip**.* — journey = the time spent moving; trip = the overall experience
- *Christopher Columbus went on a **journey** to the New World.* — long, uncertain, adventurous

---

### Key distinction

> **Trip** = the whole experience (what you did, where you went).
> **Journey** = the traveling part itself (the trayecto), especially when it was long, hard, or adventurous.
> **Travel** = the verb or the general concept of moving between places.

*The journey was tough, but we had a great trip.* — Notice how both words appear in the same sentence with different meanings.

sections.title: 1. Need Something TO vs FOR
sections.content:
The preposition after *need something* depends on what follows it.

| Follows *need something* | Preposition | Example |
|---|---|---|
| A **noun** (object / place / event) | **for** | *I need something **for** the party* |
| A **verb** (an action) | **to** + infinitive | *I need something **to** do* |

### Structure
- **Noun:** I need + [thing] + **for** + [noun] → *We need a boat **for** their holidays.*
- **Verb:** I need + [thing] + **to** + [infinitive] → *We need a car **to** go to the beach.*

### ⚠ Common mistake: 'for to'
Never combine both prepositions. Choose one or the other.
- ✗ ~~We need a car **for to** go to the beach.~~
- ✓ We need a car **to** go to the beach.

### Practice sentences
| Cue | Sentence |
|---|---|
| we / car / go to the beach | We need a car **to** go to the beach. |
| they / boat / their holidays | They need a boat **for** their holidays. |
| she / pen / the document | She needs a pen **for** the document. |
| he / suit / attend the conference | He needs a suit **to** attend the conference. |
| we / new boots / the trip | We need new boots **for** the trip. |

### Tense practice — *needed* pronunciation
- Present: *We **need** a car to go to the beach.*
- Past: *We **needed** a car to go to the beach.* — pronounce the extra syllable: **need-ed** /ˈniːdɪd/
- Future: *We **will need** a car to go to the beach.*

> *Needed* ends in D + -ed → extra syllable /ɪd/ is required. Don't swallow it.

sections.title: 2. Vocabulary: Renting a House
sections.content:
### Core verbs

| English | Spanish | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **to rent** | alquilar (pagas tú) | You are the one paying |
| **to rent out** | alquilar (cobras tú) | You are the owner receiving money |
| **rent** *(noun)* | el alquiler | *pay rent* = pagar el alquiler |
| **to book** | reservar | Short-term / holiday use only — not monthly rental |

> ⚠ **to hire** = contratar (a person). Never say *hire a flat* — the flat doesn't work for you.

### People

| English | Spanish |
|---|---|
| **landlord** | el casero / arrendador (male) |
| **landlady** | la casera / arrendadora (female) |
| **tenant** | el inquilino / arrendatario (the person who pays and lives there) |

> *Landlord* / *landlady* is one of the few English words with distinct masculine/feminine forms (like *actor* / *actress*).

### Other key vocabulary

| English | Spanish | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **deposit** | la fianza | Paid upfront at the start of a rental |
| **property / properties** | propiedad/es | *Do you rent out any properties?* |

### False friend: congress
- **congress** in English = the parliament/legislative institution of a country only
- For a professional meeting/event → always say **conference**
- ✗ ~~I have a congress tomorrow.~~ → ✓ I have a **conference** tomorrow.

### Bonus: preposition IN for attire
In English, when describing what someone is wearing (clothing or colour), always use **in**:
- *men **in** black* · *lady **in** red* · *the puss **in** boots* · *the man **in** the suit*
- Spanish uses *con* or *de*: *el hombre **con** traje* / *los hombres **de** negro*
- The English logic: the person is *inside* the clothing/colour.

### Vocabulary note: suit
- **suit** /suːt/ = traje — ⚠ not *sweet* /swiːt/ (= dulce)
- Pronounce the I as silent: **suit**, not 'sweet'.

### False friend: attend vs assist
- **attend** = asistir a un evento (ir a) — **no preposition**: *attend the conference* ✓
- **assist** = ayudar, dar asistencia — ✗ ~~assist the conference~~

sections.title: 1. Warm-Up Translations
sections.content:
Sentences translated from Spanish to English in today's warm-up.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Ojalá todo estuviera automatizado. | **I wish everything were automated.** |
| Las máquinas no se declaran en huelga. | **Machines don't go on strike.** |
| Exigen más dinero y menos trabajo. | **They demand more money and less work.** |
| Cualquier subida de salario está supeditada a un aumento en la productividad. | **Any wage increase will be tied to an increase in productivity.** |
| Sería un sueño hecho realidad. | **It would be a dream come true.** |
| Hacen lo que les dicen sin rechistar. | **They do what they're told without saying a word.** |
| Desenchúfalo antes de repararlo. | **Unplug it before repairing it.** |
| Déjame que te dé un consejo. | **Let me give you a piece of advice.** |

---

### Key Notes

**I wish + were (subjunctive):** Use *were* (not *was*) after *I wish* — this is the subjunctive mood.
- *I wish everything **were** automated.* ✅
- ~~I wish everything **was** automated.~~ ❌

**If only** works the same way as *I wish* but sounds more poetic:
- *If only everything were automated.*

**Advice is uncountable:**
- ✅ *Let me give you some advice.*
- ✅ *Let me give you a piece of advice.*
- ❌ *Let me give you an advice.*

**Rechistar** → *without saying a word* / *without complaining* / *without whining*

**Supeditada a** → *tied to* / *linked to* / *conditional on*

---

### Phrasal Verb: To Break In

**To break something in** = get something accustomed to use for the first few times.

- *I had to break in my new baseball glove.*
- *These new shoes need to be broken in.*
- *To break in a horse* = domar un caballo.

Note: **Estrenar** in English:
- Film/event → *to premiere*, *to debut*
- Clothes/shoes → *to wear for the first time*
- Shoes/gloves → *to break in* (phrasal verb)

sections.title: 2. How About · Shall · Let's
sections.content:
Three structures to **propose or suggest** something for the future.

---

### How About

Two forms:

| Pattern | Example |
|---|---|
| **How about** + *-ing* | How about going to the cinema? |
| **How about** + subject + infinitive | How about we go to the cinema? |

---

### Shall

**Only used in first person** (I / we) — never second or third.

| Pattern | Example |
|---|---|
| **Shall I** + infinitive | Shall I open the window? |
| **Shall we** + infinitive | Shall we go to the cinema? |

> ❌ *Shall you fix it?* / *Shall he come?* — NOT correct.

---

### Let's

Used in the **affirmative** (not interrogative like *shall*).
- *Let's go to the cinema.* (= Let us go…)

---

### Comparison — All Four Structures

| Structure | Example |
|---|---|
| How about + *-ing* | How about going to the cinema? |
| How about + subject + infinitive | How about we go to the cinema? |
| Shall we…? | Shall we go to the cinema? |
| Let's… | Let's go to the cinema. |
| Do you feel like…? | Do you feel like going to the cinema? |

---

### Practice Conversions

| Base | How about (*-ing*) | Shall we…? |
|---|---|---|
| buy a new one | How about buying a new one? | Shall we buy a new one? |
| fix the system | How about fixing the system? | Shall we fix the system? |
| stay at home | How about staying at home? | Shall we stay at home? |
| drive my car | How about driving my car? | Shall we drive my car? |

---

### Future Forms — Quick Overview

| Form | Use | Example |
|---|---|---|
| will | prediction, spontaneous decision | It will rain tomorrow. |
| going to | planned intention | I'm going to eat chicken tonight. |
| Present continuous | fixed arrangement | I'm eating chicken tonight. |
| Present simple | scheduled/timetabled event | I fly to Barcelona on Saturday. |
| How about / Shall / Let's | proposal / suggestion | Shall we go? |

sections.title: 3. Expressions of Frustration
sections.content:
Ways to say **estar harto / estar hasta las narices** in English.

---

### To be fed up with

*Estar harto de alguien/algo.*

- *I'm fed up with his loud music.*
- *She's getting fed up with the noise.*
- *We all got fed up with the weather.*

> ✅ Always followed by **with**.

---

### To get on one's nerves

*Poner los nervios de punta / sacar de quicio.*

- *He gets on my nerves.*
- *The loud music is getting on my nerves.*
- *Has the new boss started getting on his nerves yet?*

> ✅ No *with* — just the object pronoun.

---

### To drive someone up the wall

*Sacar a alguien de quicio / volverle loco.*

- *He drives me up the wall.*
- *The loud music is driving me up the wall.*
- *His bad habits drove her up the wall.*
- *Those new neighbours have already driven them up the wall.*

---

### To be sick and tired of

*Estar hasta la coronilla de.*

- *I'm sick and tired of the heat.*
- *She got sick and tired of me staying out so late.*
- *He never gets sick and tired of watching football.*

---

### Can't stand

*No aguantar / no soportar.*

- *I can't stand him.*
- *I can't stand the noise.*

> ✅ No *with* after *stand*.

---

### Summary Table

| Expression | Español | Followed by |
|---|---|---|
| be fed up **with** | harto de | with + noun/*-ing* |
| get on one's nerves | poner los nervios | direct object |
| drive someone up the wall | sacar de quicio | direct object |
| be sick and tired **of** | hasta la coronilla de | of + noun/*-ing* |
| can't stand | no soportar | direct object |

---

### Also useful

- *I'm fed up with putting up with my brother.* — *aguantar* = **to put up with** / **to stand** / **to bear**

sections.title: 4. Prepositions of Place
sections.content:
Prepositions describing where an object is in relation to a box.

| Preposition | Spanish | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **in** | dentro de | inside the box |
| **on** / **on top of** | encima de (tocando) | resting on the surface |
| **under** / **below** | debajo de | under the box |
| **next to** / **beside** | al lado de | touching or very close |
| **near** / **close to** | cerca de | close but not touching |
| **above** | por encima (sin tocar) | above but not touching |
| **over** | sobre / por encima | above (can also mean covering) |
| **between** | entre (dos) | between two objects |
| **among** | entre (varios) | among many objects |
| **behind** | detrás de | at the back |
| **in front of** | delante de | at the front |
| **far from** | lejos de | at a distance |
| **against** | contra (tocando) | touching the side of |

---

### Key Rules

**Near vs Near to:**
- ✅ *The ball is near the box.*
- ❌ *The ball is near to the box.*
- *Near to* is NOT used — just *near*.

**Above vs Over:**
- *Above* = strictly higher, not touching.
- *Over* = above, and can imply covering or crossing.

**Under vs Below:**
- Both mean beneath, but *below* is more about level/position on a scale.
- *Under the box* = directly beneath it.

sections.content:
Translation practice focusing on descriptive adjectives.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Hay algo suelto en el sobre. | **There's something loose in the envelope.** |
| El tornillo está demasiado flojo. | **The screw is too loose.** |
| Es un lugar muy solitario. | **It's a very lonely place.** |

title: English Time with Juls
topic: Phrasal Verb: To Get By / As If & As Though

sections.title: 1. Phrasal Verb: To Get By
sections.content:
**To get by** = apañárselas / arreglárselas — to manage in a difficult situation or with limited money.

> Non-transitive: no direct object needed — just say **I get by** or add context with *on / because / despite / somehow*.

| Pattern | Example |
|---|---|
| get by **on** + amount | *Can you get by on your salary?* |
| get by **because** + reason | *They got by because they had help* |
| get by **despite** + obstacle | *She gets by despite having little money* |
| get by **selling / doing** | *They are getting by selling postcards* |
| get by **somehow** | *We will get by somehow* |

**Rephrase practice** — simplify using *get by*:
- *They managed to survive because they had help* → **They got by because they had help**
- *I can manage with the money I earn* → **I can get by with the money I earn**
- *We will manage to survive somehow* → **We will get by somehow**

sections.title: 2. As If / As Though (Como Si)
sections.content:
**As if** and **as though** are interchangeable — both translate *como si*.

After *as if / as though*, use the **past simple** as the subjunctive equivalent — even when talking about the present.

> ⚠️ In conditional sentences, always use **were** for all subjects (not *was*):
> *I were · he were · she were · we were · they were*

**Structure:**
- *[Subject] + [verb] + as if/as though + [subject] + [past verb]*
- *It is as if/as though + [subject] + [past verb]*

**Translation practice:**

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| *Es como si tuviéramos mucho tiempo libre* | It is as if we **had** a lot of free time |
| *Él habla como si tuviera 80 años* | He speaks as if he **were** 80 years old |
| *Es como si todo el mundo estuviera de vacaciones* | It is as if everyone **were** on holiday |
| *Se mueven como si tuvieran prisa* | They move as if they **were** in a hurry |
| *Actúas como si no supieses la respuesta* | You act as if you **didn't know** the answer |
| *Es como si el fin de semana fuera interminable* | It is as if the weekend **were** never-ending |
| *Prefiero vivir como si fuese la persona más afortunada del mundo* | I prefer to live as if I **were** the luckiest person in the world |

qs.q: Which sentence uses 'to get by' correctly?
opts: I get by my salary every month.
I can get by on my salary every month.
I get by with I earn.
qs.ans: I can get by on my salary every month.

qs.q: 'To get by' is a non-transitive verb. What does that mean?
opts: It always needs a direct object after it.
It can only be used in the past tense.
It does not need a direct object.
It must always be followed by 'on'.
qs.ans: It does not need a direct object.

qs.q: Which Spanish phrase best translates 'to get by'?
Rephrase using 'get by': 'I can manage with the money I earn.'
opts: I can get by the money I earn.
I can get by with the money I earn.
I can get by for the money I earn.
I get by on earned money.
qs.ans: I can get by with the money I earn.

qs.q: In a conditional with 'as if', which is correct for all subjects?
opts: He speaks as if he was 80 years old.
He speaks as if he is 80 years old.
He speaks as if he were 80 years old.
He speaks as if he will be 80 years old.
qs.ans: He speaks as if he were 80 years old.

qs.q: 'As if' and 'as though' are…
opts: 'As if' is formal; 'as though' is informal.
Only used in the past tense.

qs.q: After 'as if / as though', which verb form do we use?
Translate: 'Prefiero vivir como si fuese la persona más afortunada del mundo.'
opts: I prefer to live as if I am the luckiest person in the world.
I prefer to live as if I were the luckiest person in the world.
I prefer to live as if I was the luckiest person in the world.
I prefer to live as if I will be the luckiest person in the world.
qs.ans: I prefer to live as if I were the luckiest person in the world.

title: Natural English
topic: Natural Reactions in Context

sections.title: 1. Goal of This Class
sections.content:
This Friday class focuses on **natural reactions** — the automatic responses native speakers use in everyday conversation.

> We often learn to *produce* language (build sentences) but rarely practice *reacting* to what others say. This class fills that gap.

The four reaction categories practised today:

| Category | Purpose |
|---|---|
| **Understanding** | Show you have understood |
| **Agreement** | Show you agree |
| **Doubt** | Express uncertainty |
| **Thinking** | Buy time before answering |

sections.title: 2. Showing Understanding
sections.content:
When someone explains something and you want to show you have understood:

| Expression | Notes |
|---|---|
| **Makes sense** | Drop *it / that* — more natural than *it makes sense* |
| **I get it** | Very common, casual |
| **Fair enough** | Accepting their reason as valid |
| **I see** | Simple acknowledgement |
| **Got it** / **Ah, got it** | Signals you have just understood |

**Example:** *"I was not at the meeting — I was not feeling well."*
→ *Makes sense · Fair enough · Got it*

sections.title: 3. Showing Agreement
sections.content:
When you fully agree with what someone said:

| Expression | Notes |
|---|---|
| **Absolutely** | Strong, enthusiastic agreement |
| **For sure** | Casual, confident agreement |
| **Couldn't agree more** | Emphatic — you agree 100% |
| **Totally** | Informal, very common |
| **Definitely** | Clear, confident agreement |
| **Exactly** | You think exactly the same |

**Example:** *"Sleeping eight hours a day is fantastic."* → agree
→ *For sure · Couldn't agree more · Totally*

sections.title: 4. Expressing Doubt
sections.content:
When you are not sure or cannot give a definite answer:

| Expression | Notes |
|---|---|
| **It depends** | The answer varies by circumstances |
| **I'm not sure** | Simple uncertainty |
| **Maybe** | Possibility, but no commitment |
| **Hard to say** | Difficult to give a clear answer |
| **I'm not convinced** | You have some doubts |

**Example:** *"Will AI replace teachers?"* → doubt
→ *It depends · Hard to say · I'm not convinced*

sections.title: 5. Buying Time to Think
sections.content:
When you need a moment before answering:

| Expression | Notes |
|---|---|
| **That's a good question** | Buys time while sounding engaged |
| **Honestly...** | Signals a thoughtful, genuine answer |
| **Let me think...** | Direct — you need a moment |
| **I've never thought about that** | Shows the question caught you off guard |
| **Off the top of my head...** | Giving an immediate, unpolished answer |

**Example:** *"What's your dream job?"* → think
→ *That's a good question · Let me think · Off the top of my head...*

qs.q: Your friend missed the meeting because of a headache. You want to show understanding. What is the most natural response?
Someone says: "Getting enough sleep is really important." You totally agree. What do you say?
Someone asks: "Will AI replace all teachers?" You are uncertain. What do you say?
You are asked: "What is your biggest fear?" You need a moment to think. What do you say?
opts: Off the top of my head...
qs.ans: Off the top of my head...

qs.q: A colleague explains why they were late and you accept their reason. What do you say?
Someone proposes an idea and you agree 100%. Which expression shows the STRONGEST agreement?

title: English with Kyle
topic: Regular Verb Pronunciation / Not As Many·As / Another · Other · The Other

sections.title: 1. Warm-Up Translations
sections.content:
Sentences translated from Spanish to English in today's warm-up.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| No camines tan rápido. | **Don't walk so fast.** |
| Se tardan 10 minutos en cruzar el río. | **It takes 10 minutes to cross the river.** |
| No íbamos rápido cuando ocurrió. | **We weren't going fast when it happened.** |
| ¿Habrá examen mañana? | **Will there be an exam tomorrow?** |
| Hoy en día, la ropa no tiene que hacer juego. | **Nowadays, clothes don't have to match.** |
| Fui corriendo detrás de ella. | **I ran after her.** |
| La alcancé en la esquina. | **I caught up with her at the corner.** |
| Tropecé con Juan en el metro. | **I bumped into / ran into Juan on the subway.** |
| Nos quedamos sin gasolina. | **We ran out of gasoline.** |
| Desenchúfalo antes de repararlo. | **Unplug it before fixing it.** |
| Dan por sentado que estamos de acuerdo. | **They take for granted that we agree.** |
| Quiero desearte mucha suerte. | **I want to wish you the best of luck.** |
| Vaya golpe de suerte. | **What a stroke of luck.** |

---

### Key Notes

**Preposition + gerund:** After a preposition, use *-ing*. → *before fixing it* (not *before to fix it*).

**Nowadays** = these days (all one word, with the A in the middle).

**To match** = hacer juego, combinar (colours, clothes). ≠ *to fit* (quedar bien de talla).

**To agree** = estar de acuerdo. This verb has no direct equivalent in Spanish — it must be expressed with a verb. *I agree. Do you agree?*

**Advice** is uncountable → *three pieces of advice* / *three tips* (not *three advices*).

**Tip** has three meanings: *propina* / *consejo* / *la punta*. → The tip of the iceberg.

---

### Phrasal Verbs: run into · bump into · come across

| Expression | Meaning | Use with |
|---|---|---|
| **run into** / **bump into** | tropezar con alguien (by chance) | people |
| **come across** | encontrar algo (by chance) | things |

- *I ran into Juan on the metro.* → met someone unexpectedly.
- *I came across some old photos.* → found something unexpectedly.

sections.title: 2. Regular Verb Pronunciation — Three Rules
sections.content:
Regular verbs in English follow three pronunciation rules for the past tense **-ed** ending.

---

### Rule 1 — Verbs ending in **T** or **D**: add an extra syllable **/ɪd/**

The -ed is pronounced as a separate syllable.

| Infinitive | Past | Example |
|---|---|---|
| last | **lasted** | The game lasted two hours. |
| decide | **decided** | They decided to go home. |
| visit | **visited** | I visited my parents last month. |

---

### Rule 2 — Verbs ending in **K, F, P, SH, CH, S**: add **/t/** sound (no extra syllable)

| Infinitive | Past | Example |
|---|---|---|
| ask | **asked** | Alberto asked me a question. |
| help | **helped** | We helped each other. |
| wash | **washed** | They washed their hands. |
| laugh | **laughed** | She laughed at the joke. |
| kiss | **kissed** | He kissed. |
| check | **checked** | I checked the answer. |

> Common mistake: saying *asked* as two syllables. It is one syllable: *asked* /æskt/.

---

### Rule 3 — All other endings: add **/d/** sound (no extra syllable)

| Infinitive | Past | Example |
|---|---|---|
| happen | **happened** | Something happened at work. |
| arrive | **arrived** | Jessica arrived last night. |
| call | **called** | The client called. |
| smile | **smiled** | The baby smiled at me. |
| prepare | **prepared** | They prepared the presentation well. |
| change | **changed** | Everything changed. |

---

### D Pronunciation — English vs Spanish

In English, the tongue **never comes out past the teeth** with the letter D. In Spanish, the D at the end of a word (e.g. *dedo*) causes the tongue to stick out — this does **not** happen in English.

Practice: *decided · did · David decided · Don does the dishes*

sections.title: 3. I Don't Think I Can
sections.content:
In Spanish **creo que no** → in English the negative moves to *think*.

| ❌ Common mistake | ✅ Correct |
|---|---|
| I think I can't go. | **I don't think I can go.** |
| I think they won't be there. | **I don't think they'll be there.** |
| I think they didn't hear it. | **I don't think they heard it.** |

**Rule:** Move the negative to the verb *think* — don't negate the second verb.

More examples:
- *Creo que no estarán allí.* → **I don't think they'll be there.**
- *Creo que no lo oyeron.* → **I don't think they heard it.**
- *Creía que no importaba.* → **I didn't think it mattered.**

sections.title: 4. Fewer · Less / Not As Many · As
sections.content:
Two ways to make a negative comparison in English.

| Structure | Use with | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **fewer** + noun | countable nouns | There are fewer cars in Palencia than in Valencia. |
| **less** + noun | uncountable nouns | There is less rain in Valladolid than in Santiago. |
| **not as many** + noun + **as** | countable nouns | There are not as many cars in Palencia as there are in Valencia. |
| **not as much** + noun + **as** | uncountable nouns | There is not as much rain in Valladolid as there is in Santiago. |

> *Not as many / not as much* is more common in everyday speech than *fewer / less*.

---

### Pattern

**Countable:** *There are not as many [noun] in X as there are in Y.*

**Uncountable:** *There is not as much [noun] in X as there is in Y.*

When using *as*, use it **twice** — once before the noun and once before the comparison.

---

### Examples from Class

- There are not as many orange trees in Catalonia as there are in Valencia.
- There are not as many traffic lights in my hometown as there are in Madrid.
- There is not as much oil in Spain as in Saudi Arabia.
- I don't earn as much money as Paul McCartney.
- There are not as many dialects in North America as there are in Africa.
- There is not as much rain in Valladolid as there is in Santiago.

sections.title: 5. Irregular Verbs — Simple Past
sections.content:
Drill: *Every day I [verb]… yesterday I [past].*

| Infinitive | Simple Past | Sample sentence |
|---|---|---|
| send | **sent** | Yesterday I sent a letter to my friend. |
| sit | **sat** | Yesterday I sat in this chair for six hours. |
| sleep | **slept** | Yesterday I slept in my bed. |
| speak | **spoke** | Yesterday I spoke about verbs. |
| spend | **spent** | Yesterday I spent money at the supermarket. |
| stand | **stood** | Yesterday I stood on the street corner waiting for a taxi. |
| steal | **stole** | They stole my money. |
| take | **took** | Yesterday I took the bus. |
| teach | **taught** | Yesterday I taught the class. (T-A-U-G-H-T → /tɔːt/) |
| tell | **told** | Yesterday I told the story. |
| think | **thought** | Yesterday I thought about it. |
| throw | **threw** | Yesterday I threw the ball. |
| understand | **understood** | Yesterday I understood the lesson. |
| wear | **wore** | Yesterday I wore a jacket. |
| win | **won** | Yesterday I won the match. |
| write | **wrote** | Yesterday I wrote a message. |
| become | **became** | Yesterday I became a better speaker. |
| begin | **began** | The class began at six. |
| break | **broke** | Yesterday I broke a world record. |
| build | **built** | Yesterday I built something new. |

---

### Steal vs Rob

**To rob** → used with people or places (the victim or location).
**To steal** → used with the thing that is taken.

| Sentence | Explanation |
|---|---|
| They **robbed** the bank. | The bank was the target. |
| They **stole** the money. | The money was taken. |
| They **robbed** me. | I was the victim. |
| They **stole** my wallet. | My wallet was the thing taken. |

> **Rule:** People get **robbed**. Things get **stolen**.

A **robbery** = *un robo*. → *There was a robbery. What did they steal?*

You cannot say *they stole me* — that would mean kidnapping.

sections.title: 6. Another · Other · The Other
sections.content:
Three related words that Spanish speakers often confuse.

---

### another (singular)
= one additional / one more (*un otro* / *uno más*)

Used with singular countable nouns. Means there is at least one more of something.

- *Would you like **another** beer?*
- ***Another** opportunity will come.*
- *I'm looking for **another** idea.*
- *Can't you find **another** solution?*

---

### other (plural)
= the plural of *another*

- ***Other** opportunities will come.*
- *I'm looking for some **other** ideas.*
- *Can't you find **other** solutions?*

---

### the other (singular) / the other ones · the others (plural)
= *el otro / los otros* — refers to a **specific** remaining item or items.

- *Give me **the other** book.* (Dame el otro libro.)
- *Where are **the other ones**?* (¿Dónde están los otros?)
- ***The others** are waiting.* (Los otros están esperando.)

---

### Summary

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Dame **otro** libro. (one more) | Give me **another** book. |
| Dame **el otro** libro. (the specific other one) | Give me **the other** book. |
| Dame **los otros** libros. (the specific others) | Give me **the other** books. |
| Quiero **otros** libros. (some different ones) | I want **other** books. |

sections.title: 7. Present Perfect — I've Never…
sections.content:
Practice: answering *When did you last…?* with the **present perfect**.

**Pattern:** *When did you last [infinitive]…?* → *I have never [past participle]…*

| Question | Answer |
|---|---|
| When did you last **win** an archery contest? | I have never **won** an archery contest. |
| When did you last **write** a letter to the president of Japan? | I've never **written** a letter to the president of Japan. |
| When was the last time you **did** something for the Zambian ambassador? | I've never **done** anything for the Zambian ambassador. |
| When was the last time you **became** ill from eating almonds? | I have never **become** ill from eating almonds. |
| When did you last **catch** a train to Copenhagen? | I've never **caught** a train to Copenhagen. |
| When was the last time a Rolls Royce **cost** less than a refrigerator? | A Rolls Royce has never **cost** less than a refrigerator. |
| When did you last **drive** my car? | I have never **driven** your car. |
| When did you last **drink** 10 litres of water in a day? | I've never **drunk** 10 litres of water in a day. |
| When did you last **have** lunch with the president of Turkey? | I've never **had** lunch with the president of Turkey. |
| When did you last **deal** with an Arab stockbroker? | I've never **dealt** with an Arab stockbroker. |

> Note: *When did you last [verb]?* uses the **infinitive**. *When was the last time you…?* uses the **simple past**.

In English, when pronouncing the letter D, the tongue…
opts: stays behind the teeth, touching the roof of the mouth
comes out past the teeth, like in Spanish

title: English Time with Juls
topic: Vocabulary About Birth

sections.title: 1. Vocabulary About Birth — Main Table
sections.content:
All vocabulary is practised inside full sentences using the **Ask Me** format.

| Word / Expression | Spanish | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **birth** (n.) | nacimiento | *The birth took place at 7 a.m.* |
| **due date** (n.) | fecha prevista / salir de cuentas | *My sister's due date is on the 7th of August.* |
| **to be due** (adj.) | estar previsto | *The baby is due on the 21st of December.* |
| **to have a nice ring to it** | sonar bien / ser eufónico | *Does the name Pamela have a nice ring to it?* |
| **to snort at sth** | resoplar / bufar ante algo | *Did you snort at his comment about the baby?* |
| **risky** (adj.) | arriesgado | *Is it risky to use too much medication for your baby?* |
| **at random** | aleatoriamente / al azar | *Will you pick your baby's name at random?* |

---

### Due Date vs To Be Due

**Due date** = noun. *My due date is the 7th of August.*

**To be due** = adjective use of *due*. *The baby is due on the 21st of December.*

> Both express a prediction / estimate, not a guarantee — that is why *due* (estar previsto) fits better than *will be born* (which sounds 100% certain).

---

### To Have a Nice Ring to It

Used when a name or word sounds pleasant, harmonious, or euphonic.

- *I really like the name Paloma. It has a nice ring to it.*
- Opposite: *That name does not have a very nice ring to it.*

> **Euphonious** (eufónico) = producing a soft, harmonious, pleasant sound — the adjective behind this expression.

---

### To Snort At

Literally: the nasal sound you make (bufar). Figuratively: to show **rejection or dissatisfaction** at a comment you do not like.

- *She snorted at his suggestion.* = resopló ante su sugerencia.

---

### At Random

= aleatoriamente, al azar.

- *They picked a name at random from the list.*
- *Do not choose at random — think carefully!*

sections.title: 2. Ask Me — Exercises
sections.content:
The class used the **Ask Me** format: the teacher gives a prompt, students form the question, then everyone repeats.

| Prompt | Question to Form |
|---|---|
| Ask me if my sister's **due date** is on the 7th of August | *Is your sister's due date on the 7th of August?* |
| Ask me if the name Pamela has a **nice ring to it** | *Does the name Pamela have a nice ring to it?* |
| Ask me if the baby **is due** on the 21st of December | *Is the baby due on the 21st of December?* |
| Ask me if I **snorted at** his comment about the baby | *Did you snort at his comment about the baby?* |
| Ask me if it is **risky** to use too much medication for your baby | *Is it risky to use too much medication for your baby?* |
| Ask me if I will pick my baby's name **at random** | *Will you pick your baby's name at random?* |

---

### Pronunciation Note — August

Stress the **first** syllable with an open sound: **AW**-gust — not *ah-GOOST*.

Practise: *August · August · August*

sections.title: 3. Extra Vocabulary — From Class Anecdotes
sections.content:
These words came up naturally during the teacher's stories about births.

| Word | Spanish | Note |
|---|---|---|
| **labour** (n.) | estar de parto | *She was in labour the whole night.* |
| **epidural** (n.) | epidural | *The doctors suggested getting the epidural.* |

sections.title: 1. Warm-Up Translations
sections.content:
Practice translating these Spanish sentences into English.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Hay una escasez de mano de obra cualificada en este país. | There's a shortage of skilled labor in this country. |
| No hay ni un solo ingeniero de caminos. | There's not even a single civil engineer. |
| Debería haber previsto ese problema. | You should have foreseen that problem. |
| Mándame un fontanero y un electricista. | Send me a plumber and an electrician. |
| El pobre hombre sufrió lesiones graves. | The poor man suffered serious injuries. |
| Tuvo varias costillas rotas. | He had several broken ribs. |
| Menos mal que estaba asegurado. | It's a good thing he was insured. |
| Abra el libro por la página cuarenta. | Open the book **to** page 40. |
| La letra de la canción. | The lyrics **to** the song. |
| El conductor estaba muerto de miedo. | The driver was scared to death. |

**Vocabulary notes:**

- **shortage** = escasez (emphasises lack; *falta* is more neutral)
- **skilled labor** = mano de obra cualificada
- **foresee / foreseen** = prever / previsto
- **plumber** = fontanero (silent B — P-L-U-M-B-E-R; possibly from Latin *plumbum* = lead, as pipes were once made of lead)
- **injury** = lesión (general); **wound** = herida (open cut); **bruise** = moratón
- **several** = varios, emphasising the quantity is large (vs *some* = algunos, neutral)

**Preposition challenge:**

- Open the book **to** page 40 — not *on* page 40.
- The lyrics **to** the song — not *of* the song (though *of* is not wrong, *to* is far more natural).

sections.title: 2. Miss vs Lose
sections.content:
Inspired by an old **Vaughan English** magazine from April 2006 with the headline:

> *"Missing Miss Loses the Plot"*

---

### TO MISS

**1. No aprovechar / no ver something** — to fail to catch, attend, or notice

| Example | Translation |
|---|---|
| I missed the bus, so I had to get a taxi. | Perdí el autobús, así que tuve que coger un taxi. |
| Due to the traffic, we missed the match. | Perdimos el partido debido al tráfico. |
| She missed three mistakes in the text. | Se le pasaron tres errores en el texto. |
| Excuse me, could you repeat? I missed that. | Perdón, ¿puedes repetir? No lo he entendido. |

**2. Miss out / FOMO**

- **To miss out** = perderse algo, no aprovechar una oportunidad.
- **FOMO** = *Fear Of Missing Out* — the anxiety of feeling you're missing something fun while others are enjoying it.

> *I don't want to go, but what if it's a lot of fun and I'm not there? I would miss out.*

**3. Echar de menos — to miss someone or something**

| Example | Translation |
|---|---|
| I miss my mother's cooking. | Echo de menos la cocina de mi madre. |
| I miss being young. | Echo de menos ser joven. |

> **Grammar tip:** After *miss*, use the **-ing** form of a verb, not the infinitive.
> - ✅ *I miss **being** with my friends.*
> - ❌ *I miss **to be** with my friends.*

---

### TO LOSE

**1. No encontrar — to be unable to find**

| Example | Translation |
|---|---|
| I've lost my keys. | He perdido mis llaves. |
| I lost the piece of paper you gave me. | He perdido el papel que me diste. |

**2. No ganar — to fail to win**

| Example | Translation |
|---|---|
| She always loses at cards. | Siempre pierde a las cartas. |

**3. Get lost = perderse**

> *When I first came to Madrid, I got lost a lot. It was pre-smartphone — I had an El Corte Inglés map in my pocket.*

**4. Lose the plot** = perder la chaveta; no entender qué está pasando

> *I've lost the plot.* = No entiendo qué está pasando aquí.

sections.title: 3. Can vs To Be Able To
sections.content:
Both express ability, but they behave differently across tenses.

| | Can | To be able to |
|---|---|---|
| Present | I **can** do it. | I **am able to** do it. |
| Past | I **could** do it. | I **was able to** do it. |
| Future | ❌ *will can* does not exist | I **will be able to** do it. |

**Key rule:** *Can* has no future form. Use *to be able to* whenever you need a future tense.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| ¿Podrá encontrarles? | Will she be able to find them? |
| ¿Por qué no podrá hacerlo? | Why won't he be able to do it? |

**Extra nuance:** *Can* often implies a **skill** or **knowledge**.

> *Can you read?* — implies knowing the skill of reading.

When *podrás* refers to a future possibility, you must switch to *will be able to*.

sections.title: 4. Mastering the Interrogative
sections.content:
Practice: given the **answer**, form the correct **question**.

| Answer | Question |
|---|---|
| The new law went into effect **last month**. | **When** did the new law go into effect? |
| The new rule has been in force **for a year and a half**. | **How long** has the new rule been in force? |
| You can stay here **as long as you want**. | **How long** can I stay here? |
| He broke it **last night**. | **When** did he break it? |
| They're expecting us **at 10 o'clock**. | **When** are they expecting us? |
| He's going to resign **later this year**. | **When** is he going to resign? |
| **This** book is mine. | **Whose** book is this? |
| **That** idea was Jennifer's. | **Whose** idea was that? |
| It depends **on you**. | **Who** does it depend on? |
| I used **the elevator on the left**. | **Which** elevator did you use? |
| The tank was emptied **by means of a pump**. | **How** was the tank emptied? |
| I got this shirt **in a small neighbourhood shop**. | **Where** did you get that shirt? |
| The bill was paid **on the 17th**. | **When** was the bill paid? |
| Nobody spoke to him because he was ill. | **Why** didn't anyone speak to him? |
| It stopped raining **shortly after lunch**. | **When** did it stop raining? |
| I used **a fire extinguisher** to put out the fire. | **What** did you use to put out the fire? |

---

**Grammar notes:**

**Whose — the noun always follows directly:**
- ✅ *Whose **book** is this?*
- ❌ *Whose is this book?* — wrong order.

**Nobody → Why didn't anyone…?**
When the statement uses *nobody / no one*, the question is more natural with a negative:
- ✅ *Why didn't **anyone** speak to him?*
- ⚠️ *Why did **no one** speak to him?* — grammatically possible but less common.

**Put out** = apagar (phrasal verb; the *out* signals extinction):
- *put out* the fire
- *blow out* the candles
- *smother out* a flame

**In effect / in force** — used interchangeably for laws and rules:
- *The law has been **in effect** / **in force** for two years.*
